entries.title: House Democrats Flub Two Big Votes After Winning Election
entries.summary: Failures to impeach Pete Hegseth and stop a veterans’ benefit cut angered rank-and-file members, but they were not blaming leaders.
entries.content:
After sweeping to election victories on the promise of fixing Washington, Democrats managed to flub two of their first votes in the House since returning to Capitol Hill, notably the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The stumbles sparked anger among Democrats, with some suggesting the party might not be ready to govern from the majority. But few were willing to point fingers at leaders who are set to run Congress next year.

“Whatever happened is unacceptable,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) told The Washington Sun when asked Wednesday whether Democrats could have prevailed in the Hegseth vote.

Another House Democrat granted anonymity to speak candidly simply said Democrats need to “get our fucking shit together.”

The other error came on Wednesday when Democrats failed to demand a roll call vote on a veterans’ bill that California Rep. Mark Takano, the top Democrat on the Veterans Affairs Committee, said would slash veterans’ benefits.

In that case, Democrats said leadership didn’t fail — it was a Republican ruse.

“It was a dirty, rotten thing to do," Rep. Rebecca Balint (D-Vermont) said. “Republicans approached our Democrat staffers on the floor and said we have technical changes to the bill."

Balint said when Takano stepped away to review the changes, Republicans called the vote.

“They did it that way because they knew they could not defend it. That tells you everything,” Takano said in a statement.

A Republican source who has directed such floor activities, however, said it’s the minority’s responsibility to not let such maneuvering happen.

“It is a fuckup by the minority leadership, plain and simple. Can’t point the finger at anyone but yourself,” the source said.

The veterans bill is not likely to pass the Senate. The Hegseth vote, though, could have led to a trial to remove a Cabinet secretary who Democrats revile.

While the lost opportunity inspired plenty of anger, Democrats were not willing to trash the leaders who will be in charge of shepherding them through what will likely be two consequential years of battling the White House.

They pointed in other directions. Several of the Democrats who missed the Hegseth vote blamed police escorts and “a traffic incident” for preventing them from reaching the floor. The office of Rep. Steven Horsford of Nevada said he had a personal emergency. Rep. Lou Correa of California was back home preparing for surgery. Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi was in San Francisco for a Veterans Day event.

Some of the harshest criticism on Tuesday came from Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California, who told reporters that members knew the vote was coming, “so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.”

On Wednesday, Kamlager-Dove simply blamed Republicans.

Minority Whip Katherine Clark, whose office is in charge of vote-counting, did not respond to questions on leadership’s role. But she told her caucus in a closed-door meeting Wednesday that Democrats had “disappointed the American people,” according to a source familiar with the matter.

Lower-ranking members of Democratic leadership declined to blame the missing members or discuss whether it could have been prevented.

“I’m not going to opine on the particular members. I don’t know the circumstances with respect to those individuals,” said Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado, who serves as assistant Democratic leader.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu of California said he wasn’t “sure what happened.”

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ office did not immediately respond to questions about the snafu.

At least publicly, rank-and-file members declined to blame party leaders who did not corral members for something as consequential as removing the defense secretary.

Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson said individual members are responsible for being on time.

“Everybody’s an adult, and they’ll have to explain back to their respective districts why they missed the vote,” Thompson said.

Even Rep.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, one of several incoming democratic socialist members who have declined to support Jeffries for speaker, blamed “structural elements” when asked if leaders were at fault.

“It’s not about an individual. It’s about a system that has not worked for the American people,” Avila Chevalier told The Sun.

Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland said the incident “will be a very important lesson for the extraordinary incoming new class.”

“There are a million events going on on the Hill and around Washington, but go to those events after you vote, not before you vote,” Raskin said

Jeffries told reporters Tuesday night that Democrats may target Hegseth again with their new House and Senate majorities. “This is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” he said.

Others shrugged it off as the kind of thing that just happens.

“I’ll take their word for it,” said Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. “Traffic can be bad. I’ve been caught in it.”

Republicans on the other hand seized on Tuesday night’s vote as a sign of things to come. “More of that’'s going to happen probably,” said Rep. Mike Simpson of Idaho.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: A Mayor in the Making
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 12, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The mayor-elect, the D.C. jail and the ‘crazy world’ of college basketball.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. Some morning showers, but mild temperatures and a chance of afternoon sunshine make this the nicest day we’ll see for a while. Read the full forecast.






THE LATEST

Earlier this fall, Janeese Lewis George sat down at Stan’s Restaurant, an unpretentious basement haunt near McPherson Square, for a regular dinner with three fellow D.C. Council members with different political views. Over drinks and fried chicken, the table raised the question hanging over her impending victory: Would she still show up once she had the veto pen?

“They were like, ‘J, are you going to be able to do this — our dinners and stuff?’” the incoming mayor recalled. “I was like, ‘We have to force me to do it.’ No matter what, don’t let the hard decisions make you ostracized from people.”

For six years, the democratic socialist has built her political brand on radical accessibility and consensus-building, The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports in an in-depth profile. Now, as the 38-year-old mayor-elect prepares to take charge of a $20 billion municipal government, one central question looms: Can she govern a fractured, fiscally strained capital without breaking the relationships that put her there?

Stepping into the executive suite means inheriting an $800 million budget deficit and confronting a job where not every crisis can be fixed. It also brings an inevitable psychological isolation. As Council Chair Phil Mendelson observed, “Individuals who become mayor risk changing their personality a bit.”

Even her closest allies acknowledge the honeymoon will end the moment her first budget lands on the dais. “The only way to maintain your integrity is you have to be willing to upset your friends sometimes,” incoming D.C. Del. Robert White said.

Asked how she plans to say “no” to the grassroots allies who powered her rise, Lewis George did not flinch.

“All I can give them is the ‘why,’” she said, “and the honesty and the integrity to look them in the eye when I do it.”


2026-11-3 Midterm Election Coverage (Washington Sun)-4 copy.jpg (2793x1862, AR: 1.50)




FROM THE DISTRICT

Labor unions aren’t happy with the autonomous vehicle bill some D.C. Council members will vote on today, even after its author, Charles Allen, made revisions aimed at appeasing them, including giving rideshare drivers and AV facility workers collective bargaining power. The Sun asked the service workers union: What is it you want to see?

Their response: a “clear legal process” that allows rideshare drivers to organize and negotiate with the companies, fair wage standards, a shared platform requirement and an explanation of exactly how workers will be protected from losing their jobs or income beyond a general displacement fund, an SEIU spokesperson told The Sun in an email.

Their requests drove key council members on the transportation committee, who are due to mark up the bill at 4 p.m., to advocate for delaying a full council vote on the issue until next session.

Inmates at the D.C. jail were among the first to see part of a forthcoming PBS documentary on crime and punishment in America. As The Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports, the film screening led to a robust discussion about the history of the criminal justice system and its impact on members of the unique audience.

The cost for replacing D.C.’s aging jail could top $2.7 billion, according to public records obtained by The Washington Post. That’s a far cry from last year’s estimate of $1.4 billion, but the city has to cough something up: Jail conditions are so poor, D.C.’s Department of Corrections is being investigated by the Justice Department.





FROM VIRGINIA

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner is still set on relocating the FBI⁠ headquarters to Virginia’s D.C. suburbs as his party prepares to regain control of Congress, the Washington Business Journal reports. His push comes as Maryland Democrats plan to revive the effort to move the headquarters to Greenbelt instead.





FROM MARYLAND

Reading between the lines: Gov. Wes Moore announced the release of his new book, “Repair,” on Wednesday. It’s set to hit shelves on March 9 and confronts how to solve America’s problems as the possible 2028 presidential candidate remains coy about running for office.

“We all know things in this country feel pretty broken right now,” Moore said in a video about the book release that he posted on X. “So this book invites us to, together, solve the hard question: What do we do about it?”





TALK TO TOM


Tom Sietsema is back, answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here. 

If you were not a food correspondent — or in the industry at all — what would you be doing right now?

Maybe working as a diplomat? A younger me aspired to go into government service, especially something that would take me abroad. (For background, I graduated from the School of Foreign Service at Georgetown.)

True story: The same question was put to me years ago during an online Q&A for The Washington Post. At the time, I responded that if I weren’t a food critic, I’d like to have a job as a morning news anchor on TV or be the head of protocol for the State Department. A week later, I got a letter from Pete Selfridge, the actual U.S. chief of protocol in the Obama administration (2014 to 2017).

In essence, the ambassador wrote, “You might want my job, but I’d like yours.”

In the full Q&A: The best mom-and-pops, replicating dishes at home and how weight-loss drugs have affected the restaurant industry. 





SPORTS

Mark Turgeon UMKC (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)
After he stepped down as the men’s basketball coach at Maryland in December 2021, Mark Turgeon was “100% sure” he was done with coaching. But five years later, he is back on the sidelines at the University of Missouri, Kansas City, a small Midwest school with no real basketball tradition. Turgeon, a Kansas native, relished an opportunity to return to the game not far from his hometown, but he also liked the idea of getting away from the complicated world of NIL and revenue sharing.

“I’m coaching players, and most of them are still doing it for the love of the game,” he told The Sun’s Alex Schiffer. “They’re not getting paid a lot. I can recruit a certain type of kid here. I’ve really enjoyed that part. I don’t feel like I’m involved in that crazy world.”

MLB general managers are gathered in Las Vegas this week for the league’s annual offseason meetings. Reporting from the desert, The Sun’s Jesse Dougherty writes that Paul Toboni, the Nationals’ president of baseball operations, articulated an offseason plan as best he could with a work stoppage around the corner.

What to Watch Today

NHL: Capitals at Devils, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

NBA: Wizards vs. Pistons, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

NFL: Commanders at Giants, 8:15 p.m. (Prime Video)

entries.title: Trump Vows to Target ‘Democrat Run Cities and States’ Post-Midterms
entries.summary: The president made several remarks on Truth Social Thursday about Democratic strongholds and immigration following Republicans’ midterms defeat.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said he would target cities and states run by Democrats in a post-midterm threat made Thursday.

“I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

The president claimed Minnesota, California, Illinois and other blue states are “poorly run, corrupt disasters,” with “Billions of Dollars is being stolen each and every month.”

Trump did not offer proof of the claims.

The midterm elections resulted in several new Democratic cities and states, including Texas and Georgia, where voters elected the first Latina and Black governors, respectively, in their state’s history.

In a separate Truth Social post, Trump said Republicans performed poorly in the midterms because he wasn’t on the ballot, a claim he’s previously made, despite telling voters at campaign rallies to cast their votes as if he were on the ballot.

Trump further claimed caravans of migrants are forming and beginning their “illegal march through Mexico.”

He implored Mexico to stop the caravans, threatening to double tariffs against the country if the caravans reach the U.S. border.

Trump said he notified Mexican authorities, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, Border Patrol and ICE.

“There will be no leniency!” Trump said.

The assertions come nearly a week after Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, stepped down and the president appointed deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller in her place.

Miller is the architect of some of Trump’s hardline immigration policies and has pushed for more corruption efforts to be aimed at Minnesota and its Somali population, The Washington Sun previously reported.

entries.title: Hegseth Honors the Soldier Who Scolded His Entourage at Arlington National Cemetery
entries.summary: The Pentagon said the defense secretary awarded the Army sentinel the Joint Service Commendation Medal.
entries.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth honored a soldier Thursday who publicly reprimanded his entourage for making noise at Arlington National Cemetery a day earlier.

“We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist,” Hegseth wrote on X, sharing photos of himself appearing to pin an award on the soldier. “Carry on Patriots.”
https://x.com/SecWar/status/2120901801281044969“As shown in the photos, Secretary Hegseth welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026,” a Pentagon official told The Washington Sun in a statement.

The recognition followed a viral video showing the soldier shouting at members of Hegseth’s group after laughter was heard near the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier during a Veterans Day event Wednesday.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the soldier yelled.

The incident drew criticism of Hegseth, with some accusing the defense secretary and his entourage of disrespecting the solemn memorial.

Hegseth had been posing for photos with his wife, Jennifer, and several senior aides, including his chief of staff, Ricky Buria. It was unclear who was laughing or whether Hegseth had made any noise.

The Pentagon said Wednesday that the soldier had acted appropriately.

“While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement.

The confrontation occurred after a wreath-laying ceremony attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is guarded around the clock by members of the Army’s 3rd Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, whose sentinels enforce strict standards of silence and respect at the memorial.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Relation-Chip Over
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Nov. 12, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Donald Trump called for GOP senators to “IMMEDIATELY” move on the $350 billion military funding bill — remember Recon 3.0? — and “deliver for our Warriors. The Democrats never will.”

  • Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin) told reporters that it’s good Trump has been “engaged” on the budget bill.
  • “The vice president’s admitted we lost because of this war and because of the gas prices,” Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) said. “So the first thing we’re going to do, with only Republican votes, is fund the Iran war. I think it’s a terrible idea.”




THE HILL

Senate Republicans are moving with haste to replace the head of the Government Accountability Office before the party surrenders power next year. The Homeland Security Committee scheduled a confirmation hearing for Nov. 19, though it did not disclose who the nominee would be, nor has the White House formally submitted a name.

Democrats greeted Rep. Jim Jordan’s election to lead the House Republican conference as evidence that the GOP is doubling down on its most extreme flank even after sweeping midterm losses. But some suggested that their party shouldn’t underestimate the Ohio Republican based on his past and his flamethrower persona.

Senate Ethics found no issue with a top staffer for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio)moonlighting as a state-level lobbying consultant, the senator’s office told The Sun.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) is defending his plans to pursue oversight investigations into the Trump administration after he got a threatening letter from a U.S. attorney with what he called “baseless” threats.






THE ADMINISTRATION

The Huang saga continues to unfold: Trump called for Tim Cook, the former CEO of Apple, to replace Jensen Huang, who resigned today as Nvidia’s chief executive.

  • House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (R-Florida) told reporters that Huang has agreed to sit before the committee before the Thanksgiving break.
  • As Howard Lutnick’s future remains uncertain, a White House official said today in a statement that the secretary’s job is safe: “President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.”
Trump says he’s pulling JD Vance off Iran talks to focus on investigating fraud, one week after the vice president blamed the conflict for poor GOP midterm showings.

Pete Hegseth honored a soldier who publicly reprimanded his entourage for making noise at Arlington National Cemetery yesterday.



THE WORLD

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the country had detected new speed restrictions on Starshield in “temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine.” SpaceX denied any change in speed.

  • “We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far, we know very little,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going.”




THE COURTS

A federal judge in Manhattan denied FIFA’s attempts to block European soccer body UEFA from seeking discovery related to president Gianni Infantino’s World Cup private investor plan. UEFA lawyers are seeking evidence from JP Morgan and Josh Kushner’s firm in the case.





PEOPLE-WATCHING-GATE

entries.title: D.C. Council Members Vote Down Self-Driving Cars, for Now
entries.summary: The five-person transportation committee nixed a bill that would have legalized autonomous vehicles in the District, citing labor and safety concerns.
entries.content:
D.C.’s transportation committee voted down a bill that would legalize passenger service in self-driving cars operated by Waymo and other companies, stalling an almost 15 year effort to bring this technology to the District.

D.C. Council members Charles Allen and Christina Henderson voted for the bill on Thursday, while Zachary Parker, Elissa Silverman and Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George voted against. In a symbolic move, as the bill would have failed regardless, council Chair Phil Mendelson — who’s allowed to vote in any committee — popped in to vote “yes.” Though lawmakers shared a general sense of support for autonomous vehicles, they disagreed about when they should be rolled out and under what conditions.

“D.C. cannot be a guinea pig,” Lewis George said in the markup, before addressing the bill’s author (and her oftentimes ally) Allen. "I do want to work with you, and I want my administration to work with you to get deployment right."

It was a victory for the members of local labor unions and D.C.’s chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, who packed the room on Thursday afternoon to voice their concerns with AV deployment more broadly.

“It’s not like we’re against technology, or against innovation, it’s just that if you’re gonna bring in this type of technology into a city to replace human being workers, you have to take the time to do it right,” Jaime Contreras, executive vice president of the local service workers union, told reporters after the markup. “That’s what we’re asking.”

Allen and other advocates for the bill took issue with the charge that it had been rushed through. The District had one of the nation’s first AV testing laws on the books in 2012. Waymo, the nation’s largest AV operator, began testing here in 2024. In the last two and a half years, the council held three public hearings on how to get the rollout right, and landed on a bill that Allen called “the most worker-friendly, the most safety-focused, the most progressive legislation” in the country.

But Allen, the committee chair, said he was not surprised by the outcome of the vote. All those who voted against the bill spoke publicly to the fact that they would earlier this week, prompting Allen to release a redrafted bill on Tuesday with major changes including giving rideshare drivers and AV facility workers collective bargaining rights, capping the total number of AVs at 800 across all companies, and introducing a requirement that all operators ensure 20% of their fleet is wheelchair accessible by 2032.

“If someone were to actually step back, read what’s in the bill, the very things they say that they want: safer streets, protections for workers, a robust regime that keeps an eye on a growing technology — they will see it in this bill. They will not see it in any other jurisdiction, and that’s what I’m going to ask my colleagues to evaluate,” Allen told reporters before unveiling the changes. “We’ll see where the chips fall.”

It wasn’t enough to sway his colleagues, or the unions who have their ears. An SEIU spokesperson told The Washington Sun that unions want to see a “clear legal process” that allows rideshare drivers to organize and negotiate with the companies, fair wage standards, a shared platform requirement and an explanation of exactly how workers will be protected from losing their jobs or income beyond a general displacement fund.

Now that the can has been officially kicked down the road, Allen and other AV advocates worry whether operators like Waymo will build out facilities in other jurisdictions or result in a revised bill without this one’s key labor or accessibility provisions.

“It’s a real risk,” Allen told reporters. “The things that we were able to get into this version of the bill, may not be as strong when Virginia or Maryland or other jurisdictions move forward.”

Waymo had already begun to build out a footprint in D.C. in anticipation of the bill’s passing, with three charging and maintenance facilities across the city, and has promised to bring hundreds of jobs to the District — one of which it’s already hiring for.

A Waymo spokesperson told The Sun in a statement that they “remain ready to work with the Council,” but warned that “postponing this debate delays the additional investments and jobs that come with scaling our operations.”

AV advocates, such as Malcom Fox of Opportunity D.C., are skeptical that council members will actually take this up in January, when the mayor-elect begins to tackle her laundry list of ambitious goals — including building 72,000 homes and navigating an $800 million deficit — while heading into budget season.

“The earliest I could really see a committee vote would be sometime in September of next year, and then it still has to go through both legislative session votes and all the things that come with it,” Fox told The Sun. “And then this bill calls for a one year advanced testing period before AVs are even allowed to operate.”

Lewis George told reporters after the markup that she will make working on this legislation a priority once she takes office.

“My hope is a group of agencies will come together to convene, to figure out how we get this right, what regulations need to be put in place, particularly our safety agencies are most concerned,” the mayor-elect said. “I’ve said time again, I’m not against AVs, I do want them to come here. I do want that innovation.”

It could mean standing opposed to the labor unions who have shown her massive support through her campaigning. As Contreras told The Sun, if he “could have it his way,” there’d be no AVs in D.C. at all.

“People have to meet me where I am, I have to meet them where they are,” Lewis George said.
